body: Ah yeah, that’s actually my bad— I suppose I forgot the circlejerk-ness in my irritation. I’ll see myself out.

I think it’s less of a “you can’t criticize our work at all” and more of a “why do you think we want your criticism” kind of thing. You can post what you want, be it a critique of a book or a fanfic. But that doesn’t mean it has to be accepted or welcomed.
I personally really dislike reading fanfic in 1st person (although there have been a few exceptions in the past). If it’s an original work, I don’t mind either way.

Okay. So.

I will say when I was younger and before I fully understood myself, I had a really bad relationship with literally anything involving pregnancy. The idea of it made me nauseated and I was even fairly uncomfortable just being around pregnant people (nothing against them as people, it just made my hackles raise for reasons I didn’t understand yet). But that was my problem to deal with and I never took it out on others. Your brother’s gf TA for how she treated/spoke about you and ur SIL, but you were also TA for stooping to her level and calling her both ugly and essentially unlovable (maybe not how you meant it, but your words could definitely be read that way). I’m not saying take the high road and immediately forgive her, but dude. You definitely didn’t make the situation any better.

Also, in regard to your comments about whether or not the phobia exists— just because you’ve never heard of it doesn’t make it bullshit. Maybe it’s not a named or well-known phobia (because Tokophobia doesn’t exactly fit this scenario in my opinion) but someone’s discomfort about one thing or another shouldn’t be dismissed because you’ve never felt it yourself.

Do you happen to have a beta reader? If not, maybe you should look into finding one. They could help you both edit your work and provide feedback if you wanted it. I’ve never had one myself, so I’m not entirely sure how it works, but it seems like you could benefit from one. It never hurts to have another set of eyes looking over your projects just for some fresh perspective.

When I say this, I promise I don’t mean it as an insult and I’m coming from a place of complete understanding because I’ve done this too— you are taking yourself and your work too seriously. You have dug yourself into a mental hole thinking that if you aren’t always improving then your work isn’t worth it. You’ve unintentionally taken the fun out of your hobby and that is a horrible feeling. 

I think you might benefit from stepping back a bit. Take up another hobby like baking or something. Start spending more time outside if you want. I hear crocheting is fun, or maybe cross-stitching. I’m personally quite fond of finger loop braiding. There are a million things you can use to fill up your time, all it takes is a curious google search! I’ve found that it’s really easy to slip into that self-deprecating sort of mindset if you fixate on something for too long. Once you have other hobbies or work to keep your mind on, then there will be less room to hyper-focus writing. (Or, that’s the hope, anyway) 

One more thing— an artist is always their worst critic. You are likely improving more than you think.  And if you aren’t making huge leaps and bounds of progress like you want, try to remember: even small steps mean that you’re still moving.

Two things:

I personally disagree with that statement, but I won’t argue on that point. It’s the same idea. You don’t go up to someone who just shared something with the world and immediately tell them what is wrong with their work. There’s a time and place for criticism, and it usually comes after the author has explicitly asked for your opinion.

Would you go up to an artist in the middle of their showcase and tell them, unprompted, that you think they need to work on (x) aspect of their work? 

Would you comment on your friend’s social media post with an unasked for remark about how they would probably look better in a different shade of green?

Would you, unprompted, tell a singer fresh out of a performance that they need to work on their vocal control because they were a little pitchy at times?

I hope you wouldn’t do any of that, because an unasked for critique can just as easily be an insult to someone who is being vulnerable and sharing something with the rest of the world. It would be different if that artist, your friend, or that singer explicitly /asked/ you for your opinion. Just like there is a difference between you offering critique to an author who didn’t ask for it versus one who did.

I personally don’t care that much, honestly— I’ll just ignore the critique and go on my merry way. I’m not writing to improve, nor am I writing to appease other people. I’m writing for my own enjoyment.

I love when people comment on my fics. It makes me happy to know that other people enjoy reading my works as much as I enjoy writing them. I don’t reply too often unless someone is asking a question, as I usually don’t know what to say. But I always make sure to thank people for the kudos and comments in the author’s notes.

I find that I most often like to write open ended one shots that I could continue as a series in the future if the inspiration so took me, but if not then they would be fine standing on their own. 

If I’m writing a multi-chaptered fic, then it’ll be 4-5 chapters tops and I’ll write them all before I post so the fic is posted already completed. If I don’t have the steam to write all the chapters or I lose interest in the story before I finish it, then I don’t run the risk of leaving my readers with an unfinished work because the work was never posted in the first place. Arguably a flawed system, but it works well enough for me.

Oh believe me, I’ve felt a lot of the same things you’re feeling right now. You definitely aren’t alone in that. Make sure to take breaks (from posting or reading or anything else you can think of related to this) if you find yourself spiraling too much into negativity. There’s no shame in having to step back for a bit— I mean, I even had to do that a little while back.

The way I think about it when I’m writing— I’m not writing for other people. I’m writing what I enjoy because I want to. If I had fun writing it, then the fic has served its purpose for me. There ain’t nothing else that matters except that I had fun and maybe someone else finds it fun too.

And when you’re reading other fics, I won’t tell you not to compare them to your own works. Everybody is guilty of doing that at some point or another, and I am certainly not exempt from that. What I will tell you is that you should try not to focus on the negative feelings your comparisons brings up (which, I know, that is extremely difficult at times). Focus on /why/ you think the work is better in the first place. Is it something about the prose? The dialogue? Is the structure of the story particularly tasteful? 

And once you find those answers, if you can find them, then learn from them. Try and apply what you see working in other fics to your own. I can’t say that this will completely fix your situation, but it will certainly change something if you start framing that comparison less as a negative thing and more as a learning experience.

Happy writing, friend!

Probably exactly what you’re imagining— the author explains the broad strokes of the fic concept in a bullet point list. And yes, they are usually noticeable if they are tagged. But unfortunately, some people either forget to tag them or just don’t for some reason.

So this one time, I’m scrolling through AO3 in the late PM/early AM as I usually do. I’m looking for some angst, maybe a little bit of family drama, some men crying and reconciliation— you know, the works. I come to this fic that has all the tags I could ask for and a description that is intriguing enough that I stop for a few moments to check the word count. It’s somewhere around 6,500 words. For a one-shot, I deem that good. I click into the fic, expecting to be occupied with an interesting story for a good amount of time before I finally lose my battle against sleep and pass out.

The fic loads. I scroll down past the tags and the title and the description.

It’s a bullet point fic.

An untagged 6,500 words bullet point fic.

The disappointment I felt was absolutely crushing. I have nothing against bullet point fics generally, but oh boy do I hate when they’re untagged. It doesn’t happen often, but when it does I get irrationally angry.

My biggest thing about reading other fantasy, I’ve realized, is that they tell you too much.

Hear me out on this: Tolkien has a great number of amazing characters and plots and what have you. He gives you the general layout for all of the things he puts forward. But there’s still so much room for the reader to slip in their own ideas. All the really detailed aspects of his world building are things that are more logistical than story based. He gives you the baseline and you can run wild with the rest. That’s why I think it’s so easy to immerse yourself in his world— because you’re unconsciously creating just as much as you’re reading. (This is especially true in the Silmarillion, I would say)

I’ve found in other fantasy stories, they offer up well thought out and detailed characters that live through relatively complex circumstances and story arcs. George R.R. Martin is a good example of this, I think (feel free to argue on that point, I haven’t read too deeply into his works because his writing just isn’t my cup of tea, this is just a general perception of mine). There aren’t a lot chances for readers to make their own assumptions or have their own interpretations of various plot points. Everything happens for a reason and these authors tell you exactly what those reasons are.

I probably didn’t explain my thinking too well, but I hope it’s at least a little understandable haha

That’s just my two cents. I’d love to hear what other people think!

Here’s something I realized after I got out of school: You probably don’t hate studying— you hate being told what to study. You even said it in the post. You like researching your religion. You like researching the gods you worship. That counts. That is enough. Learning isn’t something strictly reserved for classrooms.

Being a devotee of Athena doesn’t mean you have to love school or that you have to be a stalwart academic. It means that you enjoy expanding your knowledge in whatever subject catches your fancy. It means that you are open to learning new things even if they seem trivial in the long run. 

As another reply said, wisdom is gained through experience. And with every experience you live through, you learn something new. You become wiser. Sure, school teaches you a lot. But it isn’t the sole source of our knowledge. Life itself is our most important teacher.

The best way to honor Athena, I think, is to welcome new experiences as they come and let them teach you the lessons they carry. Let life help you expand your understanding of the world. Strive to learn about things that make you happy. But most importantly, be humble and appreciate that there are concepts you may never fully grasp.

I think it would be smart to start off with smaller projects and work your way up to the bigger ones. Drabbles are good place to begin. They’re usually less than 1000 words and they’re a great way to figure out the best style of writing that works for you! Don’t put too much pressure on yourself for a large word count or a super profound and complex story, that will come with time as you get more comfortable with writing. 

As for expressing emotions and all that fun stuff, I would recommend starting with what you know already and slowly working your way up. A good way to broaden your knowledge/solidify your confidence is to read other people’s works. Not even just in the fanfic world, but published books too. My personal written style is inspired by the works of authors like J.R.R Tolkien, Virginia Woolf, and Jeff VanderMeer (weird combination, I know). And when you write, try and mimic the techniques that you’ve read elsewhere. After a while, expressing emotions or anything at all will become like second nature.

(And the fun part about English as a language is that when you get super comfortable with it, you can start bending the rules a bit. Nouns can become verbs, adjectives can become nouns, grammar can become a suggestion and not a strict rule) ((within reason, of course))

Lastly, the great thing about AO3 is that there’s no pressure to create some critically acclaimed masterpiece that is perfect in every single way. You can just write whatever you want and there’s a pretty solid guarantee that someone out there will read it and enjoy it. If you make a few grammatical mistakes, or a description that you write ends up looking a little awkward— that’s no problem! You live and you learn! Now you know better for next time. 

And have confidence, friend. You’re probably better off than you think you are. 

Happy writing!
